# A Field Map and How to Read This Book {#sec-field-map}

The previous chapter followed one request through the stack. Now that line needs
to sit inside the whole terrain: where any topic in the book belongs, which
claims are settled and which are still argued over, where this book sits next to
the comprehensive titles already on the shelf, and why every later component is
read design-first, by asking why it has this shape and not merely what it does.
That is the map this chapter supplies.

![Schematic map of the book's terrain: measurement is firmer where systems are less coupled, and gets swampier as agentic, policy, and ecosystem effects enter. Idealized placement, not measured data.](/figures/field-map-1.svg){#fig-field-map-1}

It is organized around four questions a newcomer to the field actually asks:
where each piece goes, which parts can be trusted as fact and which are live
argument, what this book adds to the books already available, and how to read
without drowning.

## One map, eleven parts

@sec-whole-stack walked one task from raw data to a deployed agent in a single
pass. Zooming out from that vertical slice shows how the substantive parts,
Part I through Part XI, interlock. The cleanest way to hold them in mind is as a
stack: the lifecycle of a capability, with compute and data at the bottom, a
governed behavior at the top, and at every layer a set of choices that the layer
below constrains and the layer above inherits.
@fig-field-map-stack draws that stack.

```{dot}
//| label: fig-field-map-stack
//| fig-cap: "The substantive parts read as a stack. Solid arrows point from a layer to the layer built on it; dashed arrows are cross-cutting forces (evaluation feedback, safety constraints, economic pricing) that reach across layers rather than feed one into the next."
```

Read the solid arrows first; they are the build order. Part IX, the accelerators,
the networks, the data infrastructure, and the compute frontier, sits at the
bottom: it is drawn below Part I because a cluster's shape is the first constraint
on what can be trained at all (@sec-accelerators-networking,
@sec-orchestration-data-infra). Part I turns that compute into a base model by
using a @gls-scaling-law to size the run, then data curation, tokenization,
architecture, and training at scale
(@sec-scaling-laws, @sec-data-curation, @sec-tokenization,
@sec-transformer-architecture, @sec-moe-ssm-hybrids, @sec-training-at-scale). Part
II takes that same foundation in a second direction, into diffusion, flow matching,
and multimodal generation beyond text (@sec-diffusion, @sec-multimodal,
@sec-beyond-text). Part III adapts the base model to follow instructions and to
human preference (@sec-sft-peft, @sec-rlhf, @sec-dpo-variants, @sec-synthetic-data).
Part IV teaches it to spend test-time compute on reasoning
(@sec-eliciting-reasoning, @sec-training-to-reason, @sec-inference-time-scaling).
Part V is the serving problem: turning a trained model into tokens a user can
afford to wait for (@sec-serving-problem, @sec-memory-scheduling,
@sec-faster-decoding, @sec-quantization-kernels, @sec-structured-long-context). Part
VI composes served models into agents with memory, tools, retrieval, and context
(@sec-agent-architectures, @sec-memory-systems, @sec-the-harness,
@sec-multi-agent-systems, @sec-rag-retrieval, @sec-context-engineering). Part VII
measures whether any of it works (@sec-benchmarks, @sec-judging-holistic,
@sec-evaluating-agents). Part VIII reaches sideways into every layer to ask whether
the behavior can be understood, overseen, and secured (@sec-interpretability,
@sec-oversight-control, @sec-security-authorization). Part X prices the whole thing
and surveys who builds what (@sec-model-landscape, @sec-tooling-ecosystem,
@sec-economics). Part XI is the capstone: it puts the whole stack to work in
practice, from choosing a model to wiring and operating it in production
(@sec-choosing-model, @sec-wiring-stack, @sec-deployment-lifecycle).

The dashed arrows are the reason to read in order, and they are easy to miss. They
do not feed one layer into the next; they reach across the stack. Evaluation feeds
back into adaptation: a benchmark or a judge that moves changes what the next round
of post-training optimizes for. Safety constrains adaptation and orchestration
rather than sitting at the end as a coat of paint. Economics prices pretraining and
serving, and that price reaches up the stack to change design choices that look,
locally, like pure modeling decisions. Hold the dashed arrows in mind as you
read; the reading-instructions section below shows the sharpest one in full.

## Solid ground and swamp

A map is only useful if it marks the solid ground separately from the swamp, and a
reader's first defense against the noise of this field is knowing which is which.

Some of this book is settled engineering. The transformer block and its attention
mechanism [@vaswani2017attention], the autoregressive next-token objective,
attention with a key-value cache, mixed-precision training, and the basic fact that
loss falls as a smooth power law in compute [@kaplan2020scaling] are no longer in
dispute; they are the shared substrate every lab builds on. A reader can learn them
as one learns the memory model of a language: as the rules of the game, fixed for
the duration of play.

Much of the frontier is not settled, and the book marks those places rather than
papering over them. The compute-optimal ratio of tokens to parameters is a
budget-and-deployment-dependent choice, not a constant [@hoffmann2022chinchilla]
(@sec-scaling-laws). Whether reinforcement learning on verifiable rewards teaches
genuinely new reasoning or only sharpens what pretraining already put there is argued
in @sec-training-to-reason, where work like DeepSeek-R1 makes the case that pure
reinforcement learning can incentivize reasoning behavior [@guo2025deepseek]. Whether
sparse autoencoders are the right primitive for reading a model's internal features,
or a convenient but lossy lens, is open in @sec-interpretability. Whether a benchmark
number or the harness that runs it is the thing actually being measured runs through
@sec-benchmarks and @sec-evaluating-agents. The signature of the book is that these
live debates get a box, with named positions, instead of a confident sentence that
hides the disagreement. The interactive figure below draws that smooth power law: loss
falling as a straight line on log-log axes as the compute budget grows, with the
exponent set by the slider.

```{=html}
<figure id="fig-field-map-curve">
<div class="viz" data-viz="curve" data-family="powerlaw" data-xlabel="Training compute (FLOPs)" data-ylabel="Loss" data-plabel="exponent" data-pmin="0.02" data-pmax="0.12" data-p="0.07" data-logx="true" data-logy="true"></div>
<figcaption>Loss falls as a smooth power law in training compute; drag the slider to change the scaling exponent and watch the straight-line decay on log-log axes.</figcaption>
</figure>
```

::: {.callout-important}
## What's contested
The deepest open questions cluster in the upper and outer layers of the map, and
they are exactly the white space this book is written to occupy. Three are worth
naming now. First, interpretability has no agreed primitive: the superposition
hypothesis gave the field a way to think about why a model packs more features than
it has dimensions [@elhage2022superposition], and sparse autoencoders gave a
tractable handle on it [@bricken2023monosemanticity], but whether the features they
recover are the model's real computational units or an artifact of the method is
unresolved, and @sec-interpretability treats it as open. Second, the source of
reasoning gains is contested: @sec-training-to-reason weighs the claim that
reinforcement learning elicits latent capability against the claim that it installs
new capability [@guo2025deepseek], because the two imply different research bets.
Third, agent architecture has no settled form: whether long-horizon competence comes
from better memory systems (@sec-memory-systems), a stronger single-agent harness
(@sec-the-harness), or genuine multi-agent decomposition (@sec-multi-agent-systems)
is an empirical question the field has not closed. Treat any confident answer in
these three areas as a position, not a fact.
:::

## Three books, and the gap between them

A reader deciding where to spend attention deserves to know what this book is not.
Three comprehensive books already cover much of this territory well, and this book is
written to complement them rather than to repeat them. Naming them precisely is the
fastest way to say what is new here.

Chip Huyen's *AI Engineering* [@huyen2025aiengineering] is the application layer done
thoroughly: how to build products on top of foundation models you call rather than
train, covering evaluation, prompt and context design, retrieval, and deployment from
the perspective of an engineer adapting models to a use case. It treats the model
largely as a given and asks how to build well around it.

Sebastian Raschka's *Build a Large Language Model (From Scratch)* [@raschka2024build]
is the laptop-scale build: it implements a GPT-style model end to end in PyTorch, from
tokenization through attention to pretraining and fine-tuning, so a reader understands
the machine by constructing a small one. Its gift is mechanical clarity at a scale one
person can run.

Suhas Pai's *Designing Large Language Model Applications* [@pai2025designing] is the
broadest of the three, a holistic tour from the ingredients of a language model
through fine-tuning, retrieval, and agents. It covers a wide surface, and by design it
is lighter on the parts that only appear at frontier scale: at-scale distributed
training, the internals of a production serving stack, and mechanistic
interpretability.

The white space those three leave open is the middle and lower stack at frontier
scale. This book runs whole-stack, from the cluster to the agent, and spends its depth
where the others are thin: distributed training across thousands of accelerators
(@sec-training-at-scale, @sec-accelerators-networking), the internals of serving, what
actually happens inside the loop that turns a model into affordable tokens
(@sec-serving-problem, @sec-memory-scheduling, @sec-faster-decoding), and
interpretability as a first-class engineering concern rather than a research footnote
(@sec-interpretability). The aim is not to argue the other books are wrong anywhere; it
is to read the layers they pass over quickly, slowly and design-first.

## Reading instructions

The map tells you where things are. This last section explains how the chapters
are built, so the later reading requires less repeated orientation.

Every substantial chapter moves through the same arc. A chapter opens with the
**Problem**: the essential constraint the component answers, in terms of latency, cost,
memory, scale, safety, or correctness. It then gives the **Design**: the core idea that
answers the problem and the principle underneath it. **Evolution** traces how the
design got here, which earlier approaches came first and why they were superseded,
through primary sources. **Trade-offs** names what is sacrificed for what, and where
the known gaps are. **Implementation** appears only when a minimal sketch, a config, or
an operational detail clarifies the design, never to reproduce a file. Each chapter
closes with **Further reading**, first-hand sources first. The arc carries an
engineering-to-theory motion: the practice is established first, then the foundations
that explain it.

Two callouts carry the book's intellectual signature, and learning to read them is
worth the small effort. A *What's contested* box marks where the field genuinely
disagrees, with named positions, as in the box above. A *Constraint arrow* box marks
where a lower layer dictates an upper layer's choice. These arrows are the payoff of
reading the stack in order rather than dipping into chapters at random, and the next
box shows the canonical one.

::: {.callout-tip}
## Constraint arrow
The clearest single instance of a constraint arrow runs from serving up to
pretraining. @sec-scaling-laws decides how large a model to train and on how many
tokens, and read locally that looks like pure training economics: minimize loss for a
fixed compute budget, the compute-optimal recipe [@hoffmann2022chinchilla]. But if a
model will serve an enormous volume of tokens over its life, the right move is to
deliberately over-train a smaller model far past the compute-optimal point, because
training is paid once and inference is paid forever. The decision is set by the serving
cost in @sec-serving-problem reaching up the stack, not by the training budget alone.
When you meet a choice that looks unmotivated inside its own chapter, look one layer
down: the arrow that explains it usually starts there.
:::

Try changing how many tokens each model serves over its life and watch the
crossover move: a smaller, deliberately over-trained model costs more to train but
less per token, so past some serving volume it wins on total cost.

:::: {.runnable}
```python
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

# Two models assumed to reach the same quality, compared on lifetime cost.
# Training FLOPs ~ 6*N*D, inference FLOPs ~ 2*N per generated token.
big_N, big_D = 70e9, 1.4e12      # compute-optimal larger model
small_N, small_D = 13e9, 12e12   # smaller model over-trained on more tokens

served = np.logspace(11, 15, 200)  # tokens served over the model's life
big_cost = 6 * big_N * big_D + 2 * big_N * served
small_cost = 6 * small_N * small_D + 2 * small_N * served
cross = served[np.argmin(np.abs(big_cost - small_cost))]

plt.loglog(served, big_cost, label="compute-optimal 70B")
plt.loglog(served, small_cost, label="over-trained 13B")
plt.axvline(cross, ls="--", color="gray")
plt.xlabel("tokens served over life"); plt.ylabel("total FLOPs"); plt.legend()
print(f"crossover near {cross:.2e} served tokens")
plt.show()
```
::::

Two motifs recur without needing a callout, and noticing them ties distant chapters
together. The **three loops**, training, inference, and agentic, are one control
structure seen at three timescales: a weeks-long loop that turns compute into a model,
a millisecond loop that turns a prompt into tokens, and a multi-step loop that turns a
goal into actions. @fig-field-map-three-loops draws all three side by side so the
shared shape is visible: each is an input that feeds a step that produces an output
that returns to the input, and only the payload and the timescale differ.

```{dot}
//| label: fig-field-map-three-loops
//| fig-cap: "The three loops are the same control structure at three timescales. Each cycles an input through a step to an output that returns to the input, and only the payload and timescale change."
digraph {
  bgcolor="transparent";
  rankdir=TB;
  node [shape=box, style=rounded, fontsize=10, fontname="Helvetica", color="#6b7280", fontcolor="#6b7280", penwidth=1.1];
  edge [fontsize=10, fontname="Helvetica", color="#6b7280", fontcolor="#6b7280"];

  subgraph cluster_train {
    label="Training loop\nweeks";
    style=rounded;
    color="#6b7280";
    fontcolor="#6b7280";
    t_in [label="Compute and data"];
    t_step [label="Training step"];
    t_out [label="Updated weights"];
    t_in -> t_step -> t_out;
    t_out -> t_in [constraint=false];
  }

  subgraph cluster_infer {
    label="Inference loop\nmilliseconds";
    style=rounded;
    color="#6b7280";
    fontcolor="#6b7280";
    i_in [label="Prompt and KV cache"];
    i_step [label="Decode step"];
    i_out [label="Next token"];
    i_in -> i_step -> i_out;
    i_out -> i_in [constraint=false];
  }

  subgraph cluster_agent {
    label="Agentic loop\nmulti-step";
    style=rounded;
    color="#6b7280";
    fontcolor="#6b7280";
    a_in [label="Goal and context"];
    a_step [label="Action"];
    a_out [label="Observation"];
    a_in -> a_step -> a_out;
    a_out -> a_in [constraint=false];
  }
}
```

The **capability, efficiency, trust** lens closes many chapters: a technique buys
capability, or efficiency, or trust, and usually trades one against another, and naming
which it buys keeps the comparison fair.

A reader does not have to read strictly front to back. The parts are written to
interlock, so following the solid arrows of the map, pretraining before adaptation,
serving before orchestration, gives the constraint arrows their force and is the
recommended path. Reading by interest is fine too; the cross-references will point back
to whatever lower layer a chapter depends on. Either way, keep the four questions of
this chapter in hand: where it goes on the map, whether it is solid or contested, what
this book adds, and which way the arrows run.
